uses.text: Mostly used, as compounds, in herbicides, insecticides and wood preservatives (more than 80 % of U.S. use).
Very pure arsenic makes gallium arsenide semiconductors for solar cells, space and telecommunications.
Arsenic hardens lead: shot, wheel weights and battery grids.

sectors.text: Arsenic goes into solar panels, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.
Arsenic goes into the networks that carry data, data centres (storage and servers) and phones, tablets and laptops, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.

allotropes.name: Grey (metallic) arsenic
allotropes.note: Puckered layers of atoms: the stable, brittle, steel-grey form.

allotropes.name: Yellow arsenic
allotropes.note: Separate As₄ tetrahedra like white phosphorus; made by cooling the vapour quickly, and turns grey in light.

hazardStatements.text: Very toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects

Stack height 14 px. LOW PRECISION: the model abundance is small on this box's scale, so 1 px = 0.07 of the total.

bonding.note: Grey arsenic: puckered sheets of atoms, each bonded to three neighbours.

air.text: Loses its lustre in air, turning black and forming arsenic trioxide on the surface.

acids.text: Not attacked by cold sulfuric or hydrochloric acid; nitric acid or hot sulfuric acid turn it into arsenous or arsenic acid.

compounds.name: arsenic trioxide
compounds.note: the classic poison 'white arsenic'; also a leukaemia drug

biology.note: Not known to be essential for plants or for humans.

toxicity.text: Arsenate looks so much like phosphate that it enters roots through the phosphate carriers. Arsenate-tolerant races of the grass Yorkshire fog survive by taking up much less of it.

soil.text: In flooded, airless soils arsenate is turned into arsenite and much more arsenic dissolves, especially where the soil is rich in organic matter.

wild.text: Some metal-loving plants growing on mine sites and metal-rich soils accumulate arsenic, although plants do not need it.

food.text: Rice is the main food source of arsenic, above all in parts of Asia where paddies are irrigated with arsenic-rich water: arsenite slips in through the roots' silicon transporters, which rice has in abundance. Silicon fertilisers compete with it and can lower the arsenic in the grain.

environment.text: Arsenic dissolved naturally from rocks into groundwater is the greatest threat from it: wells in Bangladesh and many other countries exceed safe levels, and crops irrigated with such water carry it into food.

toxicity.text: Years of drinking water or eating food with inorganic arsenic lead to chronic poisoning, seen first in the skin as lesions and cancers.

history.discoveredText: c. 1250 (the element; its sulfides were known in antiquity)
history.nameOrigin: From the Greek arsenikon, the name of the yellow pigment orpiment (an arsenic sulfide), via the Latin arsenicum.
history.note: PubChem lists the year as 'Ancient' because arsenic compounds were known in antiquity; crediting Albertus Magnus with the element is traditional rather than certain. Schroeder published two ways of preparing it in 1649.

prose.text: Arsenic is a grey, brittle metalloid, infamous as a poison yet useful in the gallium arsenide chips of mobile phones and laser diodes. Rice can carry more of it than other cereals, because in flooded paddy soils dissolved arsenite slips into roots through the channels the plant uses to take up silicon. Heated at normal pressure, solid arsenic never melts: it turns straight into vapour at about 887 K and becomes liquid only under pressure. Like nitrogen and phosphorus above it, arsenic has three unpaired p electrons, one in each 4p orbital ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³, ground term ⁴S°₃/₂), and nature makes only one stable isotope, arsenic-75.
